cards.front: Any Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander child with middle-ear disease needs formal [___] assessment, not tympanic inspection alone.
cards.context: Every Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander child with any middle-ear disease needs their hearing formally assessed, not just their drum inspected. A normal-looking drum today does not undo months of effusion.

cards.front: Blood in stool may not be visible — perform microscopy; presence of RBCs and [___] supports inflammatory colitis.
cards.context:
Faecal occult blood may not be visible to the parent or even on gross inspection — bloody diarrhoea can present as just watery diarrhoea with subtle red discolouration or none at all.

Send stool for routine microscopy + culture in any prolonged or atypical paediatric diarrhoea.

cards.front: An itchy, relapsing rash in the skin flexures of a child with an atopic history is atopic dermatitis, commonly called [___].
cards.context: The commonest chronic childhood skin condition and part of the atopic march. Itchy, relapsing dermatitis — face/extensors in infants, flexures (elbow/knee creases) in older children.

cards.front: Infant respiratory vulnerability: smaller [___] (resistance ∝ 1/radius⁴), compliant chest walls, fewer alveoli, fetal Hb until 6 months.
cards.context:
Resistance varies inversely with the fourth power of radius — halve the diameter, sixteen-fold the resistance. So even small amounts of mucosal oedema in an infant airway dramatically increase work of breathing.

Compliant chest walls don't generate negative pressure efficiently, fewer alveoli mean less reserve, and fetal Hb's high O2 affinity slows release at the tissue level.

cards.front: Bronchiolitis = [___] episode of viral wheeze with crackles in infants under 12 months; obstruction is dominated by small-airway oedema, epithelial debris and mucus plugging.
cards.context:
A first episode under 12 months supports bronchiolitis: self-limiting viral small-airway inflammation, usually caused by RSV and managed supportively. Oedema, epithelial debris and mucus plug the small airways.

Bronchodilators are not used routinely because trials show no consistent improvement in admission or illness duration — not because infants lack airway smooth muscle.

cards.front: The first-line empirical antibiotic for paediatric community-acquired pneumonia is [___].
cards.context:
Strep pneumoniae is the dominant bacterial cause of childhood pneumonia, so empirical therapy targets it. Broaden cover only for complications or a specific suspected organism.

Dosing varies by local guidance: eTG uses amoxicillin 25 mg/kg (max 1 g) orally 8-hourly for 3 days; RCH uses 30 mg/kg (max 1 g) three times daily for 3–5 days.

Follow local severity assessment and AMS guidance.

cards.front: An infant has tetralogy of Fallot, hypocalcaemic seizures and recurrent infections. To investigate the shared genetic cause, the paediatrician orders [___] testing.
cards.context:
Conotruncal disease, hypocalcaemia and immune dysfunction together suggest 22q11.2 deletion syndrome. A cardiac diagnosis alone does not explain all three systems.

Chromosomal microarray can identify the deletion. Treat symptomatic hypocalcaemia promptly and coordinate cardiology, immunology and endocrine assessment while testing proceeds.

cards.front: A well neonate with inspiratory stridor from 2 weeks of age, worse when feeding and supine, most likely has [___].
cards.context:
Laryngomalacia presents in the first weeks of life when immature supraglottic cartilage collapses inward on inspiration.

Stridor worsens with feeding, crying, and supine positioning; most infants outgrow it by 18 months.

cards.front: After nasal trauma the septum must always be inspected, because an undrained septal haematoma devascularises the septal cartilage and causes perforation or abscess. Drainage is [___], not deferred to review.
cards.context:
Epistaxis and nasal trauma are usually benign, which is exactly why the one time-critical finding gets missed. Every child with nasal trauma needs the septum inspected.

 A septal haematoma strips the mucoperichondrium off the cartilage, which depends on it for blood supply, so untreated it necroses within days — giving septal perforation or abscess and a saddle-nose deformity.

It needs urgent drainage, not review in a week; associated fractures are reduced within 7 to 10 days.

cards.front: No chest rise while bagging a child: [___] the head, check the mask seal, open the mouth, suction, insert an adjunct, then go two-person.
cards.context:
The ladder runs cheapest-first because most failures are position or seal: re-tilt the head (neutral in infants, sniffing in children) and re-seat the mask before anything else.

Only then look inside: open the mouth, suction what you can actually see, and add a Guedel or nasopharyngeal airway if the tongue is the obstruction.

The endpoint is two-person bagging — one rescuer seals with both hands while the other squeezes. Still no rise: think foreign body or move to an advanced airway.

cards.front: Suspected concussion requires [___] from play; no same-day return to contact sport, regardless of symptom resolution.
cards.context:
'If in doubt, sit them out.' Second-impact syndrome — a second impact during the vulnerable post-concussion window — causes catastrophic cerebral oedema with high mortality.

Graduated return-to-play: ≥24-48 hours rest → light activity (no symptoms) → sport-specific exercise → non-contact training → full contact (medical clearance) → return.

cards.front: One proposed benefit of burn cooling is an [___] effect, alongside heat removal and protection of tissue.
cards.context:
Cooling may reduce inflammatory swelling, but its mechanisms are incompletely understood. Twenty minutes is a recommended first-aid regimen, not a measured anti-inflammatory dose.

The practical aims are pain relief and limiting tissue damage. Start promptly with cool running water while keeping unburnt areas warm.

cards.front: Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia produces pale stools and dark [___], because the water-soluble fraction is excreted by the kidney while no bile reaches the gut.
cards.context:
Only the conjugated (water-soluble) fraction can be filtered into urine, and only bile reaching the gut colours the stool.

So dark urine AND pale stools together is the bedside signature of a CONJUGATED (cholestatic/obstructive) picture — the pattern that demands urgent work-up for biliary atresia.

cards.front: A 9-year-old wheezes about every 3 weeks with colds and is completely well between episodes — no night waking, no exercise symptoms, no activity limitation. He fails every criterion for persistent asthma, yet a preventer trial is still worth considering, because symptoms at least every [___] define frequent intermittent asthma.
cards.context:
Every negative in the stem is doing work: no night waking, no exercise symptoms and no activity limitation rule OUT persistent asthma on all three of its criteria.

That leaves the interval as the only thing that can justify a preventer, which is why the number has to be known rather than reasoned to.

cards.front: Neisseria meningitidis appears on Gram stain as paired Gram-[___] cocci with flattened adjacent sides.
cards.context: On CSF/blood Gram stain, meningococcus is paired Gram-negative cocci with flattened adjacent sides (coffee-bean). Pneumococcus is Gram-positive and lancet-shaped — do not mix the pair.

cards.front: Most common cause of paediatric OSA is adenotonsillar hypertrophy; first-line treatment for this pattern is [___].
cards.context:
Paediatric OSA often reflects adenotonsillar hypertrophy, especially at age 2-8 when lymphoid tissue is largest relative to the airway.

For this pattern, adenotonsillectomy is first-line. It often improves symptoms and the apnoea-hypopnoea index, but residual OSA is more likely with severe disease, obesity, older age or comorbidity.

Untreated OSA can affect behaviour, growth and cardiovascular health. Persistent symptoms warrant reassessment.

cards.front: In acute asthma, start oxygen if SpO2 falls below 92% and titrate to a target saturation of [___] percent.
cards.context:
Oxygen in acute asthma is targeted, not maximal, and the trigger and target are the same across eTG, AAH and RCH.

Start supplemental oxygen if SpO2 is below 92% on room air, and titrate to a target of 92 to 96%.

Note this sits inside the severity bands: SpO2 90 to 94% is severe, and below 90% is life-threatening.

cards.front: Progressive breast development and a growth spurt are precocious when they begin before a girl's [___] birthday.
cards.context: The age threshold for precocious puberty is sex-specific: progressive secondary sexual characteristics beginning before 8 years in girls or before 9 years in boys.

cards.front: Haemoglobin is at its lifetime peak at birth — about 140-220 g/L in a term baby — and then falls to a physiological trough of roughly [___] g/L.
cards.context:
The newborn arrives polycythaemic because the fetus grows in a low-oxygen environment and compensates with a high red-cell mass.

That mass is then dismantled: fetal red cells are short-lived, and the sudden rise in arterial oxygen at birth removes the stimulus to make more.

The result is a fall of roughly half over the first two months, which is why the newborn value and the infant value look like they belong to different patients.

cards.front: Gillick competence is assessed for a [___] decision rather than granted as a general status, so a child may be competent for one treatment and not another.
cards.context:
Decision-specific, not global. The same 14-year-old may be Gillick competent to consent to a tetanus booster and not competent to consent to chemotherapy, because the second demands understanding of far more consequence.

This is why 'is she Gillick competent?' is an incomplete question. Competent for what?

cards.front: A 13-year-old boy with a BMI of 32 has a week of left knee pain and an out-toeing gait. The knee is normal; the hip is irritable and held in external rotation. Do not send him home as a knee sprain — the diagnosis is [___].
cards.context:
The file already taught that SCFE is a surgical emergency in the overweight 10–14-year-old and that hip pathology refers to the knee.

A normal knee examination with an externally rotated hip is the hinge — not 'adolescent knee pain' in general.

cards.front: Haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury after bloody diarrhoea is [___].
cards.context:
The classic triad following bloody diarrhoea (Shiga-toxin E. coli O157): microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (schistocytes), thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury.

Management is supportive — avoid antibiotics, which may worsen toxin release.

cards.front: Supracondylar humerus fracture: commonest [___] fracture in children (FOOSH 5-8y); critical complication is brachial artery injury — always check distal pulses and capillary refill.
cards.context:
Supracondylar humeral fracture is the commonest paediatric elbow fracture — classically 5-8y FOOSH with elbow extended.

Document radial pulse, capillary refill, and AIN function (OK sign) before AND after any manipulation. Untreated forearm compartment syndrome → Volkmann's ischaemic contracture (permanent flexion deformity).

cards.front: Tender red nodules over both shins, often after a streptococcal infection or with IBD, are erythema [___].
cards.context: Erythema nodosum is a septal panniculitis, a hypersensitivity reaction. Hunt for a trigger: post-streptococcal, IBD, sarcoidosis, TB, or drugs.

cards.front: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander status should be asked of [___] patient, in standard wording, rather than inferred from appearance.
cards.context:
Identification drives eligibility for the Closing the Gap PBS co-payment measure, 715 health assessments, and culturally-specific services. Missing it silently withholds all three.

Ask everyone, every time, in the standard wording — not selectively based on appearance, which is both offensive and inaccurate.

cards.front: A scaly scalp patch with broken-off hairs and patchy alopecia in a child is tinea [___].
cards.context: Tinea capitis is a dermatophyte scalp infection. It needs ORAL antifungals (griseofulvin or terbinafine) because topicals do not reach the hair follicle; a boggy inflammatory mass is a kerion.

cards.front: A major modifiable driver of retinopathy of prematurity is prolonged relative [___] during the incomplete retinal vascularisation of extreme prematurity.
cards.context:
In very preterm infants, retinal vascularisation is incomplete. Relative hyperoxia (and the subsequent hypoxic drive when oxygen is weaned) disrupts orderly vessel growth and can produce pathological neovascularisation.

Screening and oxygen targeting protocols exist because this is a leading preventable cause of childhood visual loss in ex-preterm babies — not because every brief desaturation causes it.

cards.front: In an unwell infant, falling [___] output is one of the earliest bedside markers of significant dehydration.
cards.context:
The kidneys defend circulating volume first, so output falls before sunken eyes, reduced turgor or slow capillary refill appear.

Parents can count it: fewer than 4 wet nappies in 24 hours in an infant — or no void for 6–8 hours in a toilet-trained child — signals significant volume depletion.

cards.front: A child has noisy breathing from an obstructed upper airway. Stridor is usually loudest during [___].
cards.context:
Negative pressure during inhalation can narrow an already compromised extrathoracic airway. By contrast, lower-airway narrowing commonly produces expiratory wheeze.

The sound localises obstruction, while work of breathing and air entry indicate severity.

cards.front: In children ≥2 months with suspected bacterial meningitis, give IV [___] immediately; do not delay for LP.
cards.context:
In children ≥2 months, give ceftriaxone immediately and do not delay for LP.

 RCH uses 100 mg/kg IV daily (max 4 g); eTG uses 50 mg/kg IV 12-hourly (max 2 g per dose) and notes that some centres use the RCH daily regimen. Both deliver about 100 mg/kg/day, so follow local AMS.

Younger infants require age-specific neonatal regimens.

cards.front: Before stepping up asthma therapy, check device technique and [___]; a spacer should be used with MDIs, especially in young children.
cards.context:
Most 'uncontrolled asthma' is a technique or adherence problem, not pharmacological failure — stepping up the dose just amplifies a drug that isn't reaching the lungs.

A spacer is strongly recommended — especially in young children, who can't coordinate the actuate-and-inhale timing of a bare MDI.

The spacer holds the dose as a cloud, so slow tidal breathing delivers far more drug to the airways and less to the oropharynx.

cards.front: A preschool boy has a soft, unscarred foreskin that cannot yet retract. This pattern of phimosis is [___].
cards.context:
Normal foreskin separation develops gradually through childhood. A scarred white ring or a previously retractile foreskin becoming tight suggests a different process.

Avoid forced retraction because injury can produce scarring.

cards.front: The 4 developmental domains are gross motor, fine motor, [___], and social/adaptive; global developmental delay = delay in 2 or more domains.
cards.context:
Developmental assessment evaluates four domains: gross motor (sit, walk, run), fine motor (grasp, pincer, draw), speech/language (babbling, words, sentences), social/adaptive (smile, parallel play, sharing).

Use age-specific surveillance thresholds rather than a blanket 'twice the expected age' rule. For example, not walking independently by 18 months warrants developmental assessment rather than waiting until 24 months.

cards.front: Acute hip pain in a well preschool child following a viral URTI is most likely [___].
cards.context:
Transient synovitis is a self-limiting, post-viral hip effusion. Child is well but limps or refuses to weight-bear; afebrile or low-grade fever, near-normal markers.

Always exclude septic arthritis first.

Kocher criteria (fever >38.5°C, non-weight-bearing, ESR >40, WCC >12): ≥3 of 4 → urgent USS, aspirate, theatre.

cards.front: A small pleural effusion first blunts the costophrenic angle; a larger one tracks upwards in a [___] configuration.
cards.context:
Volume determines appearance, and the progression is worth holding as a sequence.

A small effusion blunts the costophrenic angle. A larger one tracks up the chest wall in a meniscus, and fluid may also be seen within the fissures.

cards.front: Von Willebrand disease — most common inherited bleeding disorder (~[___]% prevalence); vWF has two roles: platelet adhesion + carrier protein for Factor VIII.
cards.context:
Von Willebrand disease is the commonest inherited bleeding disorder (~1% prevalence). vWF has two roles: bridges platelets to damaged endothelium (primary haemostasis) and carries Factor VIII.

vWF deficiency thus causes mucocutaneous bleeding (epistaxis, menorrhagia, easy bruising) AND mild factor VIII deficiency-like deep bleeding in severe types.

cards.front: Paediatric burn resuscitation is Parkland plus [___] fluids; the first half is due by 8 hours from the time of injury.
cards.context:
Children cannot live on resuscitation volume alone.

Modified Parkland (3 mL × kg × %TBSA in children, NOT the adult 4) runs alongside maintenance on a separate line, and the 8-hour clock starts at the burn, not at arrival.

cards.front: A 4-month-old presents in winter with 2 days of coryza followed by expiratory wheeze, fine inspiratory crackles, and increased work of breathing. The most likely diagnosis is [___].
cards.context:
A coryzal prodrome then wheeze and fine crackles in an infant under 12 months, peaking at 3-6 months in winter, is the classic picture.

It is usually caused by RSV and managed supportively, without routine bronchodilators or corticosteroids.

cards.front: The primary physiological confirmatory test for cystic fibrosis is the [___] test; a result ≥60 mmol/L is consistent with CF.
cards.context:
Cystic fibrosis is a CFTR chloride-channel disorder; sweat ducts cannot reabsorb chloride, so sweat chloride rises.

Newborn screening raises suspicion with immunoreactive trypsinogen and CFTR testing. Pilocarpine sweat chloride is the primary physiological confirmatory test; interpret it with the clinical and genetic evidence.

cards.front: Most common bacterial cause of paediatric pneumonia is Streptococcus pneumoniae; [___] is the typical 'walking pneumonia' organism in older children.
cards.context:
S. pneumoniae is the dominant bacterial cause of paediatric CAP at all ages (~30-50% when an organism is identified).

Empirical antibiotic choice reflects this: amoxicillin (typical Strep pneumo) is first-line outpatient; add/switch to azithromycin if atypical (Mycoplasma.

cards.front: Small inhaled foreign bodies lodge in the bronchial tree, affecting the [___] lobes or, on the right, the middle lobe.
cards.context:
Where the object lodges determines what happens next, and it follows bronchial anatomy.

Only large objects stay in the trachea. Smaller ones reach the bronchial tree and affect the lower lobes, or on the right the middle lobe. Undiagnosed, the child re-presents with pneumonia.

cards.front: A short 3–5-day prednisolone burst for acute asthma is stopped [___], without a taper.
cards.context:
AAH recommends a short oral prednisolone burst for acute asthma in children; three days is generally as effective as five.

Short bursts can be stopped without tapering. Longer or repeated systemic exposure needs individual review rather than a universal seven-day cutoff.

cards.front: Most limping children don't need investigations; red flag is acute inability to weight-bear; always consider [___] arthritis in severe localised joint pain with fever.
cards.context: Most limping children have benign causes (transient synovitis, minor trauma, growing pains). Red flags: complete inability to weight-bear, nocturnal pain (malignancy), systemic symptoms, duration >7 days.

cards.front: On an audiogram, bone conduction better than air conduction (an air–bone gap) signals [___] hearing loss.
cards.context:
Audiogram: O = right ear air conduction; X = left ear air conduction; brackets [ ] = bone conduction.

Diagnostic split: BC better than AC (gap between thresholds) → outer/middle ear problem (conductive — wax, OME, ossicular discontinuity, otosclerosis).

cards.front: In suspected epiglottitis, examining the throat is contraindicated because it can trigger [___].
cards.context:
Epiglottitis is a swollen, friable supraglottic airway sitting one reflex contraction away from total occlusion.

Operationally this means: do not lay the child flat, do not cannulate, do not examine the throat — keep the parent holding the child upright and call anaesthetics and ENT for a controlled airway in theatre.

cards.front: Suspected bacterial meningitis requires an agent with reliable [___] penetration, such as a high-dose third-generation cephalosporin.
cards.context:
Bacterial meningitis requires bactericidal CSF concentrations. RCH uses a high-dose third-generation cephalosporin from age two months; younger infants also receive benzylpenicillin.

Gentamicin may support bloodstream Gram-negative cover, but unreliable CSF penetration makes it unsuitable as the sole Gram-negative meningitis agent.

cards.front: First-line GDD workup starts with chromosomal microarray and [___] X testing plus thyroid and metabolic screens.
cards.context: GDD is delay in ≥2 developmental domains. First-line investigations look for chromosomal, genetic, endocrine, and metabolic causes before escalating imaging.

cards.front: An infant film shows a wide upper mediastinum. Two features argue it is a normal thymus rather than a mass: pulmonary vessels are still visible through it, and it does not [___] the airway.
cards.context:
The commonest paediatric film error is calling a normal thymus pathological, and two negative features settle it.

A normal thymus is not very radio-opaque, so pulmonary vessels remain visible through it, and it never compresses the airway or adjacent vessels. A mediastinal mass does both.

Size alone is unreliable, because the thymus involutes during acute illness and rebounds afterwards.

cards.front: IV rehydration in paediatric gastroenteritis is reserved for shock, severe dehydration, or failure to tolerate [___] fluids.
cards.context: Use enteral rehydration whenever possible. If oral ORS fails, try nasogastric ORS; reserve IV for shock, severe dehydration, or inability to tolerate NG fluids.

cards.front: Many conditions mimic seizures but are NOT epileptic; key to diagnosis is detailed history from witness + home [___] (more useful than interictal EEG).
cards.context:
Many paroxysmal conditions mimic seizures — accurate diagnosis prevents unnecessary anti-epileptic therapy.

History from witness + home video is far more useful than EEG (which is often normal between events).

cards.front: For acute asthma via MDI+spacer (RCH), a preschooler typically receives up to [___] of salbutamol 100 µg; school-age children go up to 12.
cards.context:
Salbutamol is a beta-2 agonist: it relaxes airway smooth muscle directly, relieving bronchospasm within minutes, but does nothing about the inflammation underneath — which is why a systemic steroid goes in alongside.

An MDI plus spacer delivers as well as a nebuliser in mild-to-moderate asthma and is preferred: less hypoxaemia, less tachycardia, no aerosol. Puffs go one at a time, four to six breaths after each.

The dose is stepped by size — up to 6 puffs for a preschooler, up to 12 for a school-age child — and the response to the first burst, not the count, guides what happens next.

cards.front: The infant haemoglobin trough occurs at about [___] weeks of age, because the rise in arterial oxygen after birth switches off erythropoietin production.
cards.context:
Timing is the examinable half. In a term baby the trough sits in the second and third months of life, not in the newborn period, and preterm babies reach it earlier and lower.

The mechanism explains the timing: arterial oxygen rises sharply at birth, erythropoietin production switches off, and marrow output only restarts once the haemoglobin has drifted low enough to stimulate it again.

Because it is physiological, it needs no iron and no investigation in a thriving baby.

cards.front: A large pleural effusion displaces the mediastinum [___] from the effusion, but associated pulmonary collapse may cancel the shift.
cards.context:
Mediastinal shift is the sign that tells you how much fluid there is — unless collapse cancels it out.

A large effusion pushes the trachea and mediastinum to the opposite side. Where there is associated pulmonary collapse pulling the other way, there may be no shift at all.

cards.front: A newborn has not passed meconium by 48 hours and contrast enema shows a distal transition zone. Definitive confirmation requires rectal suction [___].
cards.context:
Delayed meconium, abdominal distension and a distal transition zone suggest Hirschsprung disease, but imaging does not establish aganglionosis.

Definitive diagnosis requires histology from a rectal suction biopsy showing absent enteric ganglion cells before pull-through surgery.

cards.front: Psoriasis plaques are inflamed skin, so for a child with a few scaly plaques on the elbows and knees the GP starts the same drug class used for eczema flares: a topical [___], potency matched to site.
cards.context:
Psoriasis is less responsive than acute eczema, and in children the rule is the least potent preparation that works.

Keep potent fluorinated steroids off the face and skin folds, where thin skin absorbs more and atrophies; mild ones suit those sites.

Calcipotriol, a vitamin D analogue, and tar are adjuncts or steroid-sparing options; methotrexate and biologics are kept for severe disease.

cards.front: Well-demarcated, chalk-white depigmented macules from autoimmune melanocyte loss are [___].
cards.context: Vitiligo is autoimmune melanocyte loss, associated with thyroid disease and type 1 diabetes. Wood's lamp accentuates the patches; treatment is photoprotection plus topical steroids or calcineurin inhibitors.

cards.front: In a child aged 6–11, a post-bronchodilator FEV1 rise of at least [___]% supports asthma.
cards.context: For children aged 6–11, bronchodilator reversibility is assessed against the pre-bronchodilator FEV1. A rise of at least 12% supports variable airflow limitation.

cards.front: A five-week-old remains hungry after progressively forceful, non-bilious vomiting. A small firm mass is felt in the upper abdomen. The likely diagnosis is [___].
cards.context: Progressive vomiting in early infancy suggests gastric outlet obstruction. Early cases may lack a palpable mass or the classic biochemical abnormalities.

cards.front: Because the pyloric muscle thickens gradually after birth rather than being obstructed from day one, pyloric stenosis typically presents at [___] weeks of age with projectile non-bilious vomiting in a hungry baby.
cards.context:
Hypertrophy of the pyloric muscle builds over the first weeks of life, which is why the baby feeds normally at first and only then develops progressively forceful vomiting after feeds.

The vomit is milk, never bile, because the block sits above the ampulla of Vater. The baby stays hungry and wants to refeed at once, unlike the miserable infant with gastroenteritis.

Contrast congenital atresia, which vomits from the first day or two, and bilious vomiting at any age, which is malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise.

cards.front: The four components of tetralogy of Fallot are pulmonic stenosis, an overriding aorta, a ventricular septal defect and right ventricular [___].
cards.context:
The four components are the definition, and the outflow obstruction is what drives the radiology.

Pulmonic stenosis obstructs right ventricular outflow, so pulmonary vascularity falls and the right ventricle hypertrophies. The overriding aorta and ventricular septal defect complete the tetrad.

cards.front: Foreign body aspiration peaks at age 1-3 years; the [___] main bronchus is more commonly affected.
cards.context:
Right main bronchus is wider, more vertical, and almost a direct continuation of the trachea — gravity favours objects entering it. The 1-3 year peak reflects oral exploration combined with poor chewing.

Common objects: peanuts (most common organic), grapes, small toys. Round smooth objects can lodge at the larynx.

cards.front: After disimpaction, childhood functional constipation is maintained with an [___] laxative — usually polyethylene glycol (macrogol), not a stimulant.
cards.context:
Polyethylene glycol (macrogol) is an inert polymer that is not absorbed and holds water in the bowel lumen by osmosis, so the stool stays soft and the natural urge returns. It does not act on the bowel wall.

Persistent symptoms need review of adherence, stool burden and dose. A stimulant may be added for selected children under a treatment plan; avoid giving it against impacted stool.

Maintenance often continues for months and is reduced gradually after regular painless stools are established. Stopping too early can allow the withholding cycle to recur.
